solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Has eldest turned out to be indestructible?

indicators.note: a thing turned out in a new way is rearranged, so the letters come out in a different order

parts.note: the two words supply the letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: A parent wonders whether their oldest child has grown up to be unbreakable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' reads as 'grown up', but it is telling you to rearrange the nine letters of 'Has eldest'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that cannot die can never be destroyed, so the word is a near synonym for unbreakable or immortal.

clue.text: Chap turning on female cashier

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another comes above it, so it is written first
a thing turning faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: Sid is a stock man's name, standing for any chap
a miss is a girl or unmarried woman

explanation.surface: A man rounds angrily on the woman working the till.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cashier' looks like a noun for the till worker, but here it is the verb meaning to sack someone, especially from the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: To cashier an officer is to discharge them from service in disgrace, the same as firing them from a job.

clue.text: Cry on bishop's resignation? It will leave a hole

indicators.note: someone who resigns leaves their post, so that letter departs from the word

parts.note: to bawl is to cry loudly
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: Tears greet a bishop stepping down, and his departure will leave a gap in the diocese.
explanation.walkthrough: The bishop's departure from the cry is literal: take B out of BAWL to leave AWL.
explanation.definitionFit: An awl is a pointed tool used for punching small holes in leather or wood, so it leaves a hole behind.

clue.text: Great throw, just missing top

indicators.note: lacking a top means the first letter is gone from the word

parts.note: to heave is to throw something heavy
just and only both mean merely

explanation.surface: A sports commentator praises a throw that only just failed to hit the top of the target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just missing' reads as 'narrowly missing', but 'just' is a word to shorten, losing its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavenly is used informally to mean wonderful or delightful, a colloquial synonym for great.

clue.text: Remove Republican gatecrashing facility

indicators.note: a gatecrasher pushes into a party uninvited, so one piece forces its way inside another

parts.note: facility in the sense of ease, doing something without effort
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A call to throw out a party member who has crashed an event at some building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facility' suggests a building, but here it means ease, as in doing something with facility.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase writing or data is to wipe it out, a direct synonym for taking it away.

clue.text: Meant to be grand inside, if ornate

indicators.note: ornate means elaborately worked, so the letters are worked into a fancier arrangement

parts.note: G is short for grand, a thousand
taken as written

explanation.surface: A house was supposed to look grand inside, given its showy decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' reads as a container signal for the G, but it is fodder: G plus the letters of INSIDE and IF are all rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe what a sign or word indicates: what something signified is what it was intended to convey.

clue.text: Almost everyone on board attending a dance

indicators.note: a passenger on a vessel is aboard and so within it, meaning one piece sits inside another
almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: everyone means all of them
on board means aboard a steamship, SS, whose two letters wrap around the passengers

explanation.surface: Nearly all the passengers on a cruise ship turn up for a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attending' joins the ship-and-passengers piece to the A that follows, and the dance itself is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Salsa is a lively Latin American partner dance, so it is one example of the general category.

clue.text: Importance of figures executive originally disappearing

indicators.note: something disappearing vanishes, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: statues are sculpted figures

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of executive

explanation.surface: An executive's importance in the statistics fades from view as they leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figures' looks like numbers, suggesting STATS, but the figures here are sculptures.
explanation.definitionFit: Status is standing or prestige in a group, which is the social sense of importance or rank.

clue.text: Promiscuous and outspoken cleric, unpredictable customer

parts.note: loose is an old word for sexually promiscuous

indicators.note: outspoken here means spoken out, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a canon is a clergyman attached to a cathedral; the gun sounds the same

explanation.surface: A description of a scandalous, blunt-talking priest who no one can control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outspoken' looks like a description of the cleric's manner, but it tells you to say the word. 'Customer' is the informal British use for a person, as in 'a tricky customer'.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose cannon is an idiom for a person whose erratic behaviour may cause damage, from an unsecured gun rolling about a ship's deck.

clue.text: Organise a selection to be broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast words go out over the air and are heard, not seen

parts.note: a range is a selection of goods or options

explanation.surface: A radio producer is told to put together a mix of items for transmission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' could suggest scattering letters, but here it means said over the airwaves.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrange things is to put them in order or plan them, a straight synonym for organising.

clue.text: Sweet little thing found in harem perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small seedless dried grape
second meaning: the wife or concubine of a sultan

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet little thing' reads as a term of endearment for a woman, which fits the harem; it is in fact a dried fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a small dried grape used in baking and a wife of a Muslim ruler, who might live in his household's women's quarters.

clue.text: Girl on vacation having affair — such excitement!

indicators.note: vacation means emptying, so the inside is cleared and only the outer letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of girl
an amour is a love affair

explanation.surface: A young woman has a holiday romance and exclaims at the thrill of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' reads as 'on holiday' but means emptied out.
explanation.definitionFit: Glamour is an alluring, exciting attractiveness, the thrill a holiday romance seems to promise; 'such' points back at that whole scene.

clue.text: I had lunch outside King's Cross

indicators.note: to be outside something is to surround it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: taken as written
had lunch means ate
R is short for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone recalls eating lunch outside King's Cross, the London railway station.
explanation.walkthrough: King's Cross is a major London station, which makes 'Cross' look like part of a place name; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate and cross are both everyday adjectives meaning angry or annoyed.

clue.text: Ditching Bonn mandate perverse

indicators.note: perverse means contrary or twisted, so the letters are twisted into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A headline says scrapping an order from the old West German capital was wrong-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: Bonn was the capital of West Germany, which makes the clue read like politics; 'Ditching' is the noun-like definition at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Ditching, as an act, is dropping or giving something up, which is what abandonment names as a noun.

clue.text: Huge waste ending in ruin of philosopher

parts.note: epic means on a huge scale
urea is a waste product of the body, passed in urine

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of ruin

explanation.surface: A thinker's downfall comes from vast extravagance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste' suggests squandering money, a fitting fate for a pleasure-seeker, but it is bodily waste.
explanation.definitionFit: An Epicurean is a follower of Epicurus, the Greek thinker who taught that pleasure and freedom from pain are the highest good.

clue.text: Composer angrily rails at heartless court

indicators.note: an angry outburst throws things about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: without its heart a word loses its middle, keeping just the outer letters

parts.note: the outside letters of court, which is also its standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A musician furiously denounces a cruel and unfeeling royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rails at' means scolds, so it reads as part of the story; it supplies seven letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Domenico Scarlatti was an Italian baroque composer known for his keyboard sonatas; his father Alessandro also composed.

clue.text: Wordy tome His Eminence has taken into house

indicators.note: to be taken into a place is to be brought inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: Taurus is one of the twelve astrological houses
HE is the abbreviation for His Eminence, a cardinal's title
has shortens to 's, as in he's

explanation.surface: A cardinal has had a long, verbose book brought into his residence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' suggests a building, but in astrology the signs of the zodiac are called houses.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesaurus is a reference book full of synonyms, so it is quite literally a tome made of words.

clue.text: Expose stomach for audience

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word is meant to be heard rather than read

parts.note: to stomach something is to bear or tolerate it

explanation.surface: A performer shows off their midriff for the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stomach' looks like the body part being shown, but it is the verb meaning to put up with.
explanation.definitionFit: To bare something is to uncover it or lay it open to view, which is what exposing does.

clue.text: Dish of sturgeon occasionally expensive in France

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of sturgeon
cher is French for expensive (and for dear)

explanation.surface: A plate of sturgeon, the caviar fish, sometimes costs a lot in a French restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish of sturgeon' looks like a menu item, but 'of' is a link and only the plate is defined.
explanation.definitionFit: A trencher is an old wooden platter or board on which food was served and cut, so a kind of plate.

clue.text: Old queen lazed around?

parts.note: to laze is to have done nothing, so the verb part of that phrase is supplied
O is a round letter, and it doubles as zero, the nothing done

explanation.surface: A former monarch idled about her palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lazed around' is read as 'did nothing', DID plus O for nothing; the question mark flags the loose, playful parse.
explanation.definitionFit: Dido was the legendary queen of Carthage, abandoned by Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid, so an ancient monarch.

clue.text: Some in Paris concealing failing schemes

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide something within, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: des is French for some, as in des pommes
a vice is a moral failing

explanation.surface: A few Parisians are hiding their unsuccessful plots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Failing' looks like an adjective for the schemes, but it is a noun meaning a fault.
explanation.definitionFit: Devices can mean plans or tricks, as in 'left to his own devices', a slightly old-fashioned sense of schemes.

clue.text: Scrap university competition to secure new expedition vessel

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece holds another inside

parts.note: to scrap a thing is to end it
U is the standard abbreviation for university
a race is a competition
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A university cancels a contest meant to pay for a new research ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secure' reads as 'obtain funding for', but it means hold inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance was Ernest Shackleton's ship on his 1914 Antarctic expedition, crushed by pack ice and found on the seabed in 2022.

clue.text: Called for work to block river Dee

indicators.note: a blockage sits inside a channel, so one piece is lodged within another

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, a crossword favourite
an act is a deed or piece of work
dee is the spelt-out name of the letter D

explanation.surface: Engineering works are demanded to dam the River Dee.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dee is a real river in Wales and Scotland, so 'river Dee' reads as one name; 'river' is one piece and 'Dee' is just the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To exact something is to demand and obtain it, as in exacting payment, so exacted means required or demanded.

clue.text: Right place for a quarrel?

parts.note: surface reading: a suitable venue for having an argument
setter's reading: a quarrel is also a square-headed crossbow bolt, and this is the case an archer keeps such missiles in

explanation.surface: Someone asks where would be a fitting spot for a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarrel' means an argument to almost everyone, but it is also an old word for a crossbow bolt.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the archer's case for arrows and bolts, the proper place to keep such projectiles ready.

clue.text: Crazy Sunday with VIP, drinking this?

definitions.note: the definition points at the answer through the clue's scene; it is what is being drunk

indicators.note: crazy means wild and disordered, so the letters go wild into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wild Sunday spent in the company of a celebrity, with a glass in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: what might you be drinking on such a day?
explanation.definitionFit: Vin de pays is a French category of local country wine, a step above table wine, so a plausible thing to be sipping.

clue.text: District hospital defended by old man

indicators.note: a thing defended is guarded on all sides, so it sits within its protector

parts.note: a sire is a father, an old man in the slang sense
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A local hospital is protected by an elderly gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' reads as an elderly man but is slang for father, and a father is a sire.
explanation.definitionFit: A shire is a county or administrative district in Britain, such as Yorkshire or Hampshire.

clue.text: Relative in detention centre an Indian copper once

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so only that single letter is kept

parts.note: the fifth of the nine letters of detention
an anna was a former Indian coin, made of copper, worth a sixteenth of a rupee

explanation.surface: A family member is held in custody along with an Indian policeman from the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detention centre' reads as a prison and 'copper' as a policeman; in fact it is the middle letter and a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Nanna is a familiar British name for a grandmother, so a family member.

clue.text: Chopper to take off without His Majesty? On the contrary

indicators.note: without can mean outside, so one piece would surround the other
this flips the stated order, so the surrounding role passes to the other piece

parts.note: CR stands for Carolus Rex, King Charles, the current monarch
to take off is to leave or depart

explanation.surface: A helicopter is told to depart without carrying the King.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as written, the departing would go outside the monarch; 'On the contrary' swaps the roles so the royal initials wrap the leaving. 'Chopper' is slang for a helicopter, but here it is a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleaver is a heavy butcher's knife for chopping meat, so it is a chopper.

clue.text: Sister might appear thus to people

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: a nun appears dressed in her habit
second meaning: to people a place is to live in it

explanation.surface: A nun is likely to look this way to the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People' looks like a noun, the people the sister appears to, but it is a verb meaning to populate.
explanation.definitionFit: To inhabit a region is to occupy it as residents, just as to people it is to fill it with inhabitants.

clue.text: Writer's unfinished work? I don't like it

indicators.note: something unfinished is missing its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a writer's work is a book

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses an author's incomplete manuscript with a curt verdict.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole spoken phrase: the cry an audience makes at something it dislikes.
explanation.definitionFit: Boo is the noise of disapproval a crowd makes, which amounts to saying they dislike what they see.

clue.text: Old carouser settled youngster's case

parts.note: to have settled on a seat is to have sat

indicators.note: a case is the outer covering, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of youngster

explanation.surface: An elderly reveller pays off a young person's legal claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settled' and 'case' together suggest a lawsuit, but they work separately.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth satyrs were drunken, lustful woodland creatures who followed Dionysus, the classic ancient party animals.

clue.text: Two promises becoming a curse

parts.note: the first promise: a verb meaning to vow
the second promise: a pledge, as in giving one's word

explanation.surface: A pair of vows that turn into a burden or misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curse' suggests a spell or affliction, but here it is a profanity.
explanation.definitionFit: A curse in the sense of an oath or obscenity is an offensive word, an expletive.
